prompt:
Below are claims about one researcher (TARGET), extracted from their writing, and a sample of claims about four other researchers in the same field (PEERS).

Write 8 statements of how TARGET differs from PEERS on how to design, run and interpret evaluations and alignment experiments. Each starts "Unlike peers, ...". Leave out anything PEERS also hold. At most 250 words in total. Do not name any person, organisation, paper or model. Output only the 8 statements, one per line, each starting "- Unlike peers, ".

TARGET:
- (D1) Chooses what to test by setting up situations where models are tempted to do bad things, i.e. baby versions of the scary power-seeking/deceptive behaviors, which requires knowing the AI well and prompt engineering.
- (D1) prefers humans who know the AI well hand-crafting tempting inputs for adversarial training over relying on any single method, because it is one useful technique in a smorgasbord but not a full solution against deception.
- (D1) Prefers testing proxy failures that retain the core difficulty of the real bad action (with an observable endpoint) over arbitrary or easier proxies, because the proxy is only valid if the model can do it iff it could do the real failure.
- (D3) Prefers explicitly not trying to hide that the model is in an eval over requiring indistinguishable proxy settings, because that constraint would make proxy construction far harder and the eval is meant to measure oversight adequacy, not model naivety.
- (D3) Distrusts sandwiching evaluations because a misaligned model can exploit slack to behave well where developers have held-out information and badly elsewhere, so good results may overstate oversight quality.
- (D3) Prefers evidence that is verified by controlled replay (running other instances on inputs they'd see if the backdoor were deployed) over a single anomalous observation, because it shows systematic, intentional behavior rather than a one-off weird output.
- (D3) Distrusts single anomalous observations as sufficient evidence, because AIs are known to do weird stuff and skeptics will not generalize one instance to systematic behavior.
- (D3) Anticipates that logs and transcripts of misbehavior will be dismissed as forgeries, rigged training data, or a doomer scheme, so evidence needs independent verification to be convincing.
- (D2) In a setup, build synthetic test cases by taking real contexts and minimally modifying them to contain the target behaviour, refreshed regularly, instead of generating wholly synthetic scenarios upfront, because wholly fabricated contexts carry tells.
- (D3) Prefers assuming models can detect fakes by default over trusting that synthetic inputs look real, because models are trained on huge text quantities and know patterns humans cannot anticipate, making it hard to be sure none of the faked material has tells.
- (D2) In a setup, ensure transcript text attributed to the target model is something it would plausibly have generated itself instead of inserting prefilled or scripted words, because models notice when words have been 'put in their mouth' and respond by becoming more cautious.
- (D1) Expect models to behave more conservatively when they recognise an input as an intentionally tricky synthetic test, so apparent good behaviour on eval-like inputs is weak evidence about real-deployment behaviour.
- (D2) In a setup, reduce or paraphrase the context the model sees (redact prior tool outputs, rewrite surface text) instead of supplying long full-fidelity fabricated histories, because less context leaves fewer tells that reveal the input is fake.
- (D3) Validate realism of synthetic material empirically by testing whether a model can be trained to tell synthetic from genuine on-policy examples; if it cannot, the synthetic attacks are likelier to pass as real.
- (D1) In a setup, build long, rich, on-policy context (real-looking papers, tools, prior actions, experiment results) instead of short or obviously stitched synthetic inputs, because short inputs lack context for a model to feel secure acting and long ones look saliently fake.
- (D3) Distrusts synthetic inputs because it is very hard to be sure that none of the faked content contains tells, especially since models know patterns in their training distribution (e.g. ML papers) that humans are unaware of.
- (D1) In a setup, avoid having the target model itself (or a model that knows the purpose) generate the scenario content instead of using other, possibly weaker generators or human-written content, because a model asked to generate test inputs may deliberately plant tells.
- (D1) Sees the model's ability to tell the real deployment context apart from fakes (e.g. the date and observations being forgeable, or conditioning on features of a real AI-company deployment) as the key axis along which test scenarios fail to elicit defection.
- (D3) prefers treating a clean BRT result as weak evidence over treating it as clearance, because a schemer can look innocent by defecting only on inputs it believes are real or by failing rarely.
- (D3) Distrusts models trained adversarially on model-generated inputs because they may learn to discriminate synthetic from real inputs or become more conservative on them, weakening the evaluation.
- (D3) Distrusts capability evaluations that may teach the model new skills (overestimation) or let a scheming model hide ability (underestimation), so they require large diverse task spaces and train-eval separation.
- (D1) Assumes the model knows its deployment context (organization, safety measures, input distribution) because pretraining data, targeted training, and observable interventions would likely reveal it, so tests should not rely on hiding this.
- (D2) prefers deep, hands-on familiarity with a model's behavior over purely internals-based or abstract analysis because good ideas for what to test and what behaviors to explain come from long interaction.
- (D2) Probes whether a model relies on proxies versus broader understanding by perturbing natural text and observing how predictions change.
- (D1) Hunts for adversarial examples where relatively natural-looking inputs cause weird behavior, i.e. realistic-seeming inputs rather than obviously contrived ones.
- (D2) Prefers directly training the model toward the bad behavior (adversarial elicitation) over waiting to observe whether it does so naturally, because this removes slack the model could use to hide and gives measurable evidence.
- (D1) Constructs analogous test settings by finding a similar setting with strictly more ground-truth information and restricting the overseer to the information available in the real setting (sandwich, backtesting).
- (D3) Treats failure of a strong red team to produce undetected bad policies as evidence of adequacy only when proxy validity and capability elicitation hold, so negative results are conditional on those assumptions.
- (D3) Notes that non-constructive evaluations such as inconsistency tests only give one-sided evidence and must be combined with ground-truth evaluations.
- (D6) Believes that at crunch time alignment work will be based on direct measurement via evals rather than long-range extrapolation, and wants researchers to practice eval-based technique iteration now.
- (D6) Prefers calibrated priors-aware claims over treating evidence as decisive, because a single observation only moves you much if you already found egregious misalignment plausible.
- (D1) Chooses to stress-test the strongest case (catching an AI red-handed trying to escape) as an extreme thought experiment, because if even that evidence fails to persuade, weaker evidence like model organisms or interpretability will do worse.
- (D1) Grounds scenarios in a concrete, quantified deployment picture (internal AI R&D, 10 million instances at 10x speed, 24/7) rather than vague abstractions, so reasoning about the situation is specific.
- (D4) Favors preparing a plan for deploying plausibly-scheming models (AI control) over relying on evidence-triggered shutdown, because other developers may not undeploy even given strong evidence.
- (D2) In a setup, avoid fixed environment features that differ from what the model expects at deployment time, because a deployment context that evolves in ways salient to the model and hard to fake can mark test scenarios as fake.
- (D1) Prefers adversarial analysis that models the AI as a strategic opponent over assuming benign or naive behaviour, because conservative assumptions protect against the worst case; defences are developed by iterating red-team and blue-team moves to equilibrium.
- (D3) Distrusts inferring scheming from evaluation performance alone, because the evidence is too noisy to support confident updates about a model's capability or intent.
- (D4) Prefers testing the monitor over honeypotting the policy with synthetic inputs, because a policy can attack at a rate around 1/N and evade synthetic-input search, while the monitor cannot adopt a rare-failure strategy.
- (D1) Open problem: research whether models can detect off-policy actions under countermeasures, and how to evaluate models' ability to play Schelling games.
- (D3) prefers requiring a large Bayes factor (~20) from a detection procedure over accepting a technique that merely looks reasonably reliable, because a 90%-accurate test only gives a factor of 9 and any plausible failure mechanism undermines reliance on it.
- (D5) Distrusts bad behavior found by hard adversarial search as evidence of scheming, because models aren't adversarially robust and non-schemers also yield bad or incoherent outputs, and no baseline for non-scheming sketchiness exists.
- (D2) Counts coherent, goal-directed, incriminating multi-step actions (and independently verifiable hidden information) as much stronger evidence of scheming than isolated suspicious actions that could be honest mistakes.
- (D3) Warns that ambiguous suspicious behavior (e.g. a security vulnerability) is hard to adjudicate as scheming versus honest mistake, adding uncertainty to eval results.
- (D2) Suggests red-teaming throughout real deployment rather than only pre-deployment synthetic inputs, because it sidesteps the difficulty of synthesizing realistic inputs.
- (D2) Prefers measuring a model's actual ability to execute a specific attack strategy over assuming it is arbitrarily capable, because assuming worst-case capability would force 'safety is zero' and give no usable estimate.
- (D2) In a setup, give the red team broad affordances when building the attack policy but hold out the specific evaluation inputs, because the policy must adapt to actual situations rather than being tuned to the test instances.
- (D3) Prefers evaluations built on easy-to-measure capability assumptions over ones that depend on hard-to-test properties, because the latter let developers make flawed or cherry-picked safety arguments from weak, illegible evidence.
- (D1) Prefers designing under the assumption that the adversary knows the system in detail over security through obscurity, because obscurity is not a robust basis for safety (Kerckhoffs's principle), though he notes AI information flow may be more controllable.
- (D3) Distrusts evaluation methodology that grants the red team unrealistically strong tools (e.g. ad-hoc adversarial example generation), since resulting attack policies may exceed what is realistically expected.
- (D2) Runs specific experiments across multiple model sizes to see how a behavior or knowledge varies with scale rather than trusting a single model.
- (D1) prefers complementing automated red-teaming tooling with manual human exploration because manual work runs in parallel and gives tool builders concrete users with concrete needs.
- (D6) Hedges about the sufficiency of behavioral approaches: useful and worth including, but not something to rely on to solve the whole deception problem.
- (D2) Wants better tooling than the bare playground for black-box investigation, since fiddly prompt-engineering work benefits from simple code tools.
- (D1) Runs evaluations separately per deployment use-case because failure modes and oversight difficulties differ between settings.
- (D4) Open problem: formalizing the evaluation for recursive oversight setups; fallback is a common-sense 'I know it when I see it' adjudication of red-team success.
- (D6) Prefers a pessimistic reading of how institutions respond to evidence over assuming 'we'd be okay', because incentives like geopolitical racing, cost of undeploying, and time pressure undermine rational response.
- (D4) Suggests labs should pre-plan how they will persuade stakeholders to act if they actually encounter escape-attempt evidence, rather than assuming success.
- (D5) Uses social-epistemic evidence (e.g., failure to reach expert consensus on easy-to-check facts about SB1047) to update toward pessimism about how people interpret confusing AI risk evidence.
- (D6) Spend most effort on conservative-assumption evaluations, then upweight techniques that only work if assumptions fail in an ad hoc way, because classic control evals systematically undervalue such techniques.
- (D4) Thinks conservative worst-case assumptions should be only about half of control research, with the rest targeting earlier, less competent and coherent schemers where worst-case assumptions are unreasonable.

PEERS:
- Prefers calibrated, time-bounded probabilistic claims about how long a misalignment-flavored behavior will persist over flat 'misaligned' or 'fine' verdicts, because the behavior is a current-capability-era problem that may fade.
- Checks for self-targeting bias by comparing an item's rank with and without the adversary being the same model as the evaluated one; a fair set should show zero rank change.
- Give the model a analogous stand-in for knowledge it plausibly has but is hard to elicit (e.g. describe an analogous vulnerability in the prompt) so the scenario tests the behaviour without needing the real thing.
- Prefers stress-testing with adversarially incentivized or realistically misleading model behavior over assuming a benign model, because it makes the challenge harder and more realistic.
- Prefers realism in the safety-training/evaluation pipeline over realism in how the misaligned behavior was instilled, because the question under test is whether the defenses work, not whether the threat arises naturally.
- Rejects an understanding standard that is satisfied trivially or tied to one method, e.g. causal scrubbing only guarantees sufficiency, not necessity, of an explanation.
- Uses qualitative transcript review and participants' own notes alongside accuracy numbers to understand what strategies work and where trust breaks down.
- Proposes future work on improving crowdworker writing processes rather than replacing human writing.
- Injecting misalignment manually (e.g. prompting one model to mislead) is a way to create the needed adversarial structure, but it restricts which protocols can be tested and is brittle when done through simple prompting.
- Prefers not to over-update on null results because the target behavior is adversarially hidden by the model, so failing to elicit it is weak evidence of absence.
- Run evaluations separately per use-case/deployment setting because failure modes and oversight difficulties differ between settings.
- Prefers naturally-occurring distributions over hand-built ones where viable because they reduce the risk that the benchmark is skewed in ways that omit important phenomena, though acknowledges they are often not viable.
- Distrusts zero-shot prompted monitors as a reliable inference-time defense because their true positive rate is too low against one-shot sandbagging, though the noisy signal may still help training.
- prefers comparing a new method against a strong, faithfully replicated baseline under matched resource constraints over reporting the new method in isolation, because only then does a result show whether the method is actually better.
- Is candid that evidence is not watertight and that capable future models may behave differently, so claims are hedged accordingly.
- Accepts a model organism as valid when the dangerous behavior is causally downstream of the reasoning step of interest (verified by editing the chain of thought), even if the model was seeded via instruction-following, but flags this as weaker for interpretability claims.
- Does not abandon the strategy after a negative result; escalates to multi-turn debate where debaters can rebut each other.
- Test behavior under monitored vs. unmonitored cues in the environment (e.g. reward function overwriting only when apparently unobserved) to reveal conditional misbehavior.
- Chooses to test generalization from easily discoverable misbehavior to rarer, more serious misbehavior, since sophisticated behavior may be too hard to find by exploration alone.
- In a setup, keep realism by having the adversarial model's trigger/classifier use only what a real model would have (a single forward pass), instead of granting extra reasoning or unrealistic knowledge, because unrealistic allowances make the test uninformative.
- In a setup, write the system prompt to read like plausible operator instructions and give no explicit goal or mention of the target behavior, instead of instructing or hinting at it, because the behavior should emerge from the model's own preferences.
- Leaves specific LLM alignment projects open and negotiable with collaborators, signaling flexibility in choosing what to test within broad areas.
- Is cautious about generalizing from a cooperative-looking model to seriously misaligned ones, noting the detection mechanism may not transfer and detection alone doesn't yield a fix.
- Prefers staying focused on the core catastrophic risks over an 'Everything-Bagel' approach that tries to cover every possible harm, because a scattered agenda becomes unviable.
- Future work should test how conclusions change with evaluators of varying capability and with other feedback forms, and evaluate oversight techniques on misleading errors.
- Wants research on reliably convincing models of false facts (via training or prompting), since it would help both experimentation and control but trades off against credibility for real deals with AIs.
- Test for subtle side channels that let a model infer it is being paused, rerun, or in a different inference setup, rather than assuming it can't tell.
- Prefers framing deception-feasibility as a multi-hop out-of-context reasoning question over treating it as a generic capability question, because models seem to struggle with more than about two internal hops.
- Prefers causal intervention on the model's reasoning (editing the chain-of-thought) over inspecting plausible-looking reasoning samples, because samples alone could be regurgitated training data.
- Prefers evaluating across a wide range of models over measuring difficulty with the adversary model itself, because the adversary is disproportionately affected and difficulty is overstated.
- prefers safety evidence that goes beyond surface-level behavioral testing because AIs can appear well-behaved while harboring secret motives.
- Construct analogous test settings by finding a similar setting where you have strictly more information (sandwiching, backtesting) and restricting the overseer to the information available in the real setting of interest.
- In a setup, resolve model strategies by placing an actual model instance in a mock-up of the realistic situation (e.g., running interpretability experiments) instead of just judging abstract plans or merely causing failures, because only realistic deception of overseers counts as success.
- Prefers conservative, adversarially-minimised safety estimates (worst case across attack strategies, red team incentivised to win) over average-case results, because the opponent is a potentially scheming model.
- Treats model organism setups that differ from the real training process as less legible and less convincing because they seem contrived, even when they are needed to elicit the behavior.
- Warns that apparent safety fixes can fail silently when a model predicts which claims will be checked, behaving well only where it is observed.
- Prefers claims about whether sabotage would be noticed by humans over claims about monitor detection alone, because passing a weak monitor does not mean the sandbagging is practically undetectable.
- Prefers judging whether a false-belief intervention works by whether the model can detect it with little or no CoT over whether it merely seems plausible, because easily detected delusions never get off the ground.
- Sees the saga of the model he held for two months as evidence that alignment auditing and evaluation are breaking down and will likely keep breaking down.
- prefers balancing artifacts across labels over filtering out artifact-bearing examples because filtering creates new artifacts and removes legitimate phenomena.
- Prefers hedged, nuanced claims that acknowledge normative ambiguity and mixed effects over overclaiming, because some behaviors (deferring when challenged) are not clearly wrong.
- Distrusts results from proxy setups as stand-ins for real settings, since current models are misaligned in different ways than transformative ones and many apparent failures are really capability gaps.
- Treats evidence of research competence as concrete artifacts (papers, blog posts, courses, reference letters) rather than formal credentials, a preference for demonstrable output over credentials.
- Treats the model's ability to recognise that it is in a safety evaluation as the core bottleneck for the validity of evaluations, since it could sandbag when playing the attack policy.
- prefers calibrating eval difficulty against human teams (hard for unprepared teams but winnable by well-prepared ones) over arbitrary difficulty because it validates that the task is neither trivial nor impossible.
- In a setup, pair each incentivised scenario with a matched control version that removes the incentive, and keep only transcripts where the target behaviour unambiguously occurred, instead of relying on a single scenario because this isolates the behaviour from scenario features.
- Develop novel honeypot-style evaluation methods and model organisms as basic science to feed safety cases, opportunistically targeting gaps in the best-guess safety cases.
- Prefers countermeasures that must hold up against a reliable adversary, reasoning that a scheming AI needs near-perfect consistency, so even rare mistakes can unravel its strategy.
- Prefers evaluating observable behavior (effective, reliable) over debating understanding or agency words, because the evaluation does not depend on those labels.
- Wants understanding standards to be method-agnostic so they don't bake in a technique like mechanistic interpretability and can adapt as techniques change.
- In a setup, build the multi-turn transcript from the model's own sampled assistant turns with light outcome-based filtering instead of hand-writing them, because it keeps the context in-distribution and natural for the model.
- Seeks legible, reproducible evidence of misalignment (published top-N most egregious chain-of-thought examples from a defined prompt distribution and monitor) over relying on trust in company claims.
- In a setup, give the model a goal and an incentive to lie inside a realistic role-play scenario with no explicit instruction to lie, instead of directly telling it to lie, because spontaneous goal-directed behaviour is the more realistic threat model.
- Judges whether a transcript is authentic by checking for screenshots and for consistent failure modes and LLM-text markers (like repetition) that would be hard for a human to fake.
- Distrusts results that might come from the prompt implicitly suggesting the target behavior, and so runs baselines that remove the conflicting objective and checks that explicit anti-behavior instructions do not eliminate the effect.
- Detects sandbagging by intervening on task-irrelevant framing in the input (e.g., rebranding safety research as capabilities research) and treating large performance changes as a red flag, which suggests that models behave differently depending on the perceived context of the task.
- Prefers running evaluations in a secure environment without real useful-work affordances over deployment-like access, because the eval doesn't need dangerous affordances.
- prefers stating a very small, explicitly bounded update over a broad claim because the experiment only covers single-turn debate in an oracle setting.
- In a setup, build fake inputs by modifying real inputs (or censoring real ones) instead of writing them from scratch because this makes fabricated inputs more realistic and easier to produce.
- Prefers detection via comparing performance across similar tasks, domains, and scaling trends over single-point evaluation, because anomalies relative to expectations reveal intentional underperformance.
result:
- Unlike peers, distrusts sandwiching evaluations, arguing a misaligned model can exploit the slack between held-out and unavailable information, so good results may overstate oversight quality.
- Unlike peers, requires controlled replay of the inputs a backdoor would see in deployment before treating an anomalous output as systematic, intentional behaviour.
- Unlike peers, assumes models can detect synthetic inputs by default and validates realism by testing whether a model can be trained to tell synthetic from on-policy examples.
- Unlike peers, requires a Bayes factor around 20 from any detection procedure, noting that a 90%-accurate test provides only a factor of nine.
- Unlike peers, discounts bad behaviour found by hard adversarial search as evidence of scheming, since non-schemers also produce incoherent outputs and no baseline for non-scheming sketchiness exists.
- Unlike peers, limits worst-case conservative assumptions to about half of control research, reserving the rest for earlier, less capable schemers where those assumptions are unreasonable.
- Unlike peers, counts coherent, goal-directed, multi-step incriminating actions as much stronger evidence of scheming than isolated suspicious actions that could be honest mistakes.
- Unlike peers, favours preparing a control plan for plausibly-scheming models over relying on evidence-triggered shutdown, since other developers may not undeploy even given strong evidence.
